segments.text: Alright, to continue our series about wildlife, today I'll be talking about the rhinos in
Kruger, one of South Africa's national parks.
I'll go through some problems the rhinos are facing, some new ways to help them, and
some threats to our mission.
First, let me show you some statistics.
Currently, there are fewer than 4,000 rhinos in Kruger, compared to over 10,000 in 2010.
The population is divided between 3,549 white rhinos, those are grazers with square lips,
and 2,068 black rhinos, which have pointed upper lips that help them pluck leaves and
fruit from trees.
Kruger's rhinos account for about 30% of the world's estimated 18,000 wild rhinos.
The number of rhinos in Kruger has declined by approximately 70% in the last 10 years.
This is mainly due to poaching.
Poachers hunt rhinos for their horns because they are used in traditional medicine or carvings,
mostly in China and Vietnam.
The largest number of rhinos killed by poachers was recorded in Kruger in 2014 when over
800 rhinos were slaughtered for their horns.
The second largest reason are the knock-on consequences of poaching on breeding and calf
survival.
Specifically, the poaching of rhino cows has been doing harm to the population because
each female may give birth to as many as 10 calves in her lifetime, and calves without
their mothers often die due to predators or hunger.
Another reason for the decline in the number of rhinos is climate change.
A drought that stretched through 2015 to 2016 caused further losses.
Rhinos bred less, and dehydrated mothers produced less milk, causing malnourished calves to
die.
During the drought, food was scarce, and white rhinos were particularly hard hit by
the lack of grass to eat.
They died at twice their normal rate, according to South Africa's Department of Environment
Forestry and Fisheries.
So what measures have been taken to protect the rhinos, you may ask?
Despite the grim news overall, targeted surveillance technology in the park, which often focuses
on saving breeding-age females, and some high-level arrests of poachers have been helping.
According to Sandparks, poaching was reduced by 21.6% between 2018 and 2019, and also
elephant poaching declined by 43.8%.
Another way to protect rhinos is to move some of them from Kruger to safer areas, such
as other national parks.
This strategy has been stalled for years, however, because of an outbreak of tuberculosis
among rhinos.
Perhaps many of you have heard of dehorning, a common anti-poaching strategy in which
park rangers saw off rhinos' horns so that they have no value to poachers. This method is only
applied to small private parks since it can be extremely expensive. It requires a helicopter,
a skilled veterinarian, and costs between 600 and 1000 dollars per rhino. Moreover,
it's not a one-time solution because the horns grow back every few years.
The threats that lie ahead are not to be considered lightly. Poachers are still the
biggest enemies of Rangers. Or are they? As evidenced by arrests, poaching gangs have
clearly been able to infiltrate the Ranger force within Kruger, along with other parks and reserves.
Sandparks calls internal corruption a scourge and says it severely impacts staff and anti-poaching
operations, as well as Sand Park's reputation.
